source_refs.note: PDF 264-265 (book p. 262-263): sec x domain and range, Figure 9.12, principal secant function, sec^-1 domain and range, Figures 9.13(a) and 9.13(b)

blocks.text: The graph of the function \(f(x) = \sec x\) with domain \(\left\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R} \wedge x \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\) and range \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\) is shown in Figure 9.12.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
\(\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}\), so we must remove every \(x\) where \(\cos x = 0\): the odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) (\(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \dots\)), written \((2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\). These are the vertical asymptotes of the graph.
As with cosecant, \(|\cos x| \le 1\) gives \(|\sec x| \ge 1\), so the range is \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1) = (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = sec x for x from minus 5 pi over 2 to 5 pi over 2. Dashed vertical asymptotes at the odd multiples of pi over 2. Dashed horizontal lines y = 1 and y = minus 1. Branches opening upward have lowest points (minus 2 pi, 1), (0, 1) and (2 pi, 1); branches opening downward have highest points (minus pi, minus 1) and (pi, minus 1).
blocks.caption: Figure 9.12: graph of \(y = \sec x\) from \(-\frac{5\pi}{2}\) to \(\frac{5\pi}{2}\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure; the point at \(x = \pi\) is correctly labelled \((\pi, -1)\))

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the book's Figure 9.12 the point at \(x = \pi\) is labelled \((\pi, 1)\). Since \(\sec\pi = \frac{1}{\cos\pi} = \frac{1}{-1} = -1\), the point is \((\pi, -1)\), the top of a downward branch (just like \((-\pi, -1)\)). Our drawing shows the correct label.

Clearly from the graph it follows that secant function is not bijective because the line \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\) touches the graph at many points. However, if we restrict the domain of \(f(x) = \sec x\) to the interval \([0, \pi] - \left\{\frac{\pi}{2}\right\}\), then the function with restricted domain i.e. \(f : \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right] \to (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\) becomes one-one and onto (bijective) that is invertible and is called principal secant function. The inverse secant function is defined by

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book writes 'if' here. As for every other inverse function in this unit, the definition works in both directions, so it should read
\[y = \sec^{-1} x \iff x = \sec y\]
(iff = if and only if), with \(y \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \([0, \pi]\)? It is the same interval we used for \(\cos^{-1} x\). On \([0, \pi]\), \(\cos x\) decreases steadily from 1 to \(-1\), taking each value once. Its reciprocal \(\sec x\) rises from 1 to \(+\infty\) on \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and from \(-\infty\) up to \(-1\) on \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\): each value with \(|y| \ge 1\) once. Only \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) has to go, because \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\).
Because the interval matches cosine's, \(\sec^{-1} x = \cos^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) (Example 4 in 9.1.6).
The domain of \(\sec^{-1} x\) is \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\) and range of \(\sec^{-1} x\) is \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\).

The graph of the function \(\sec : \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right] \to (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\) is shown in Figure 9.13(a) and graph of \(\sec^{-1} : (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty) \to \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\) is shown in Figure 9.13(b).

blocks.alt: Principal branch of y = sec x on 0 to pi. From the point (0, 1) the curve rises to plus infinity as x approaches pi over 2 from the left. To the right of the dashed asymptote x = pi over 2 the curve comes up from minus infinity to the end point (pi, minus 1).
blocks.caption: Figure 9.13(a): graph of \(y = \sec x\) from 0 to \(\pi\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of y = inverse secant of x. For x at least 1 the curve starts at (1, 0) and rises towards the dashed line y = pi over 2 without reaching it. For x at most minus 1 the curve starts at (minus 1, pi) and falls towards y = pi over 2 without reaching it. Dashed horizontal lines y = pi over 2 and y = pi.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.13(b): graph of \(y = \sec^{-1} x\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Reading the two graphs: reflecting Figure 9.13(a) in \(y = x\) gives Figure 9.13(b). The end points swap: \((0, 1) \to (1, 0)\) and \((\pi, -1) \to (-1, \pi)\). The vertical asymptote \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) becomes the horizontal asymptote \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\): \(\sec^{-1} x\) comes as close as we like to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) for large \(|x|\) but never equals it. For \(x \ge 1\) the values lie in \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\); for \(x \le -1\) they lie in \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick example of our own. \(\sec^{-1} 2 = y\) means \(\cos y = \frac{1}{2}\) with \(y \in [0, \pi]\), so \(y = \frac{\pi}{3}\).
\(\sec^{-1}(-2) = y\) means \(\cos y = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(y = \frac{2\pi}{3}\) (not \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\): negative angles are outside the range of \(\sec^{-1}\)).
\(\sec^{-1}(-1) = \pi\) and \(\sec^{-1} 1 = 0\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}\); domain \(\mathbb{R} - \left\{(2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\right\}\), range \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).
2. Principal secant function: \(\sec : \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right] \to (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).
3. \(y = \sec^{-1} x \iff x = \sec y\).
4. Domain of \(\sec^{-1} x\): \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\); range: \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\).
5. \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\) is a horizontal asymptote of \(\sec^{-1} x\); its values are never negative.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Giving a negative answer for \(\sec^{-1}\) of a negative number, e.g. \(\sec^{-1}(-2) = -\frac{\pi}{3}\). The range of \(\sec^{-1}\) is inside \([0, \pi]\); the answer is \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\).
2. Including \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) in the range: \(\sec\frac{\pi}{2}\) is undefined.
3. Confusing \(\sec^{-1} x\) with \(\frac{1}{\sec x} = \cos x\).
4. Mixing up the intervals: \(\sec^{-1}\) uses cosine's interval \([0, \pi]\), \(\csc^{-1}\) uses sine's interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
